items.title: Can criticising a CJI stop you from becoming a lawyer? | LME shorts
items.summary: Several NALSAR students objected to Chief Justice of India Surya Kant being invited as the chief guest for their convocation. Their protest followed a Supreme Court hearing on July 22 concerning protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar over alleged police action against protesters. The Bar Council of India then briefly blocked the entire 2026 graduating batch from enrolment with State Bar Councils, while seeking details about those who organised the campaign. But can the BCI actually prevent law students from becoming lawyers simply for opposing or criticising a CJI? Our latest LME Shorts breaks down the NALSAR-CJI controversy, the BCI’s powers and what happened after the enrolment order was withdrawn.

items.title: Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 gets President's assent
items.summary: President of India Droupadi Murmu on August 13 gave her assent to the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026, which seeks to overhaul the administration and functioning of tribunals across the country and create a new National Tribunals Commission (NTC). The Bill was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 10 without discussion amid Opposition protests. The Rajya Sabha passed it a day later. The Act seeks to make the tribunal system more independent, transparent and uniform. It also repeals the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, several provisions of which were struck down by the Supreme Court for giving excessive control to the executive over tribunals. The new law follows a series of Supreme Court judgments, including the Madras Bar Association v. Union of India cases, concerning the independence and functioning of tribunals. Key provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026: National Tribunals Commission The Act establishes aims to establish a National Tribunals Commission (NTC) to oversee 16 tribunals, including the Central Administrative Tribunal, the National Green Tribunal, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, the Armed Forces Tribunal

items.title: Commercial Courts Act 2015 applies to commercial suits filed before its enactment: Delhi High Court
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has held that the restrictions on appeals under the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 apply even to commercial suits filed before the law came into force. [Yes Bank v. Modi Rubber] A three-judge Bench of Justices V Kameswar Rao, Chandrasekharan Sudha and Amit Mahajan ruled that litigants in such suits cannot claim the wider appellate remedies available under the earlier legal regime merely because the proceedings began before October 23, 2015. "We hold that the provisions of the Commercial Courts Act shall be applicable to suits filed prior to its commencement, even if the suits were converted or re-numbered into commercial suits only on a later date," the judgment stated. The ruling came on a reference arising from an appeal filed by Yes Bank against a March 2019 order that allowed Modi Rubber Limited to amend its plaint in a recovery suit. The suit was filed in 2014 for recovery of ₹33.13 crore with interest and damages. It arose from credit facilities extended by Yes Bank in connection with a joint venture between Modi Rubber’s subsidiary and Continental AG. Although the suit preceded the Commercial Courts Act, it was renumbered as a commercial suit only in 2020.
